title: Takht Hazur Sahib
hook: at Nanded, where he passed the Guruship to the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takht Patna Sahib, in the east, by the Ganges. Your line was where he was born. Whose birthplace did you ask about, and what small detail stayed with you? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

Draw a line on a map of India. Start at Patna in the east, where the Tenth Guru was born. Swing it west to Anandpur in the hills of Punjab, where the Khalsa began. Then drop it a long way south, across the middle of the country, to a town on the Godavari river called Nanded. The line of his life doesn't end where it started, or where most of his story happened. It ends in the south, far from Punjab. We stood at Nanded once before on this path, for his last days. Today we come back to the place itself, and to the Takht that stands there now.
screen: `PATNA, ANANDPUR, NANDED.` → `A LIFE DRAWN ACROSS A MAP.` → `IT ENDS IN THE SOUTH.`

segments.voice: Takht Hazur Sahib stands at Nanded, by the Godavari. Hazur is a word of respect, used for being in the presence of someone great, and Sikhs often call the place simply Hazur Sahib. Its fuller name speaks of Sachkhand, the realm of truth, and Abchal Nagar, which Sikhs render as the steady, unmoving city. Now the history the Takht keeps. Tradition says that here, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh did not name a person to follow him. He bowed before the Granth and passed the Guruship to it. From that day, Sikhs say, the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa gathered before it as the Guru Panth. So Patna holds the beginning of one life, and Nanded holds the end of that life and the beginning of something without an end. A person can be born, and a person can die. The Granth was given to stay. That's why Sikhs speak of this Takht with such weight. It marks the hand-off. It also marks how far the panth reaches. Patna in the east and Nanded in the south are both Takhts, and both sit far from Punjab, which some readers take as a quiet reminder that the Guru's house was never meant to belong to one province. Pilgrims come by train and bus from all over to bow where the hand-off happened. Where he gave the guruship.
screen: `HAZUR: IN THE PRESENCE.` · `NO PERSON NAMED NEXT.` · `THE GURUSHIP GIVEN TO THE GRANTH.` · `A TAKHT FAR FROM PUNJAB.` · then, large: `WHERE HE GAVE THE GURUSHIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the Godavari river. Settle, and breathe. See a wide river moving slowly through flat land, under a big southern sky. Let the water keep moving past you without hurrying. A river can't be held in one place; it goes on after anyone who stands beside it. Let that be the whole thought. If you pray, you can rest in the Guru's presence by the water. If you don't, let the river carry your breath along until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Takht Hazur Sahib. The seat of authority at Nanded, by the Godavari, where tradition says the Tenth Guru passed the Guruship to the Granth. Today's word.
Your line: where he gave the guruship. Today, notice one thing you've been holding that could be handed on, a task, a skill, a key. Hand it on well. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.
